issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot direct a lower court to make an independent fresh municipal valuation where the governing statute assigns valuation to the municipal authority and provides no statutory basis for judicial valuation.
material_facts: The municipal authority assessed the premises using a valuation method that the lower courts held was not the applicable method.
The Small Causes Court set aside the assessments and directed fresh valuations by the municipal authority.
After the statutory time for the authority to make a fresh valuation had expired, the High Court remanded the matter so the Small Causes Court could itself ascertain the annual value.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s remand for the Small Causes Court to make a fresh valuation was invalid and was set aside; the Small Causes Court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Rates create a statutory liability, which can arise only from a valuation made in the manner provided by the statute. The statute did not contemplate a valuation made independently by a court. The court could not use inherent power to direct an act that the statute did not authorize, or disregard a statutory consequence to prevent the municipal authority from losing rates. The Court referred to Governor-General of India in Council v. Corporation of Calcutta, 51 C.W.N. 517; North British & Mercantile Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, Case No. 6 of 1943 (unreported); and Corporation of Calcutta v. Chandoo Lal Bhai Chand Modi, 57 C.W.N. 882.

predicates.appeal_from_municipal_valuation: A ratepayer appealed a municipal authority’s valuation of property.
predicates.original_valuation_cancelled: The original valuation was set aside rather than retained with adjustments.
predicates.appellate_court_directed_lower_court_to_: An appellate court directed a lower court to determine a new valuation itself.

issues.definition: When a ratepayer appeals a municipal valuation, the original valuation is set aside, and an appellate court directs a lower court to make a fresh valuation, the remand for judicial valuation is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A court’s direction to create a fresh valuation from the beginning is not a revision or alteration of an existing valuation.
material_facts: The original valuation used one method, while the valuation contemplated by the High Court would use a different method.
The High Court directed the Small Causes Court to ascertain the annual value itself, rather than to modify figures or other elements in an existing valuation.
The original valuation had been set aside.
issues.conclusion: The proposed judicial valuation could not be treated as a revised or altered valuation under the statutory provisions governing revision and its consequences.
issues.legal_principle: A valuation is revised or altered when an existing valuation is retained with modifications, such as changing its underlying figures or allowing a different depreciation. Creating a new valuation from the start, without reference to an existing valuation, is not revision or alteration within sections 147 and 164 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923. The Court disapproved Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal v. Corporation of Calcutta, 58 C.W.N. 537, and referred to Governor-General of India in Council v. Corporation of Calcutta, 51 C.W.N. 517; North British & Mercantile Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, Case No. 6 of 1943 (unreported); and Corporation of Calcutta v. Chandoo Lal Bhai Chand Modi, 57 C.W.N. 882.

predicates.appeal_from_municipal_valuation: A ratepayer appealed a municipal authority’s valuation of property.
predicates.original_valuation_cancelled: The original valuation was set aside rather than retained with adjustments.
predicates.new_valuation_created_from_the_start: The proposed valuation would be determined anew without modifying or relying on the existing valuation.

issues.definition: When a municipal valuation is appealed, the original valuation is set aside, and a new valuation is created from the start, the proposed valuation is not a revision or alteration.

issues.legal_issue: A valuation made contrary to the statutory method is an irregularity for purposes of the statutory provision authorizing a fresh valuation after cancellation.
material_facts: The municipal authority used a valuation method that the courts held was not applicable to the premises.
The Court of Small Causes set aside the valuation on that basis.
The municipal authority argued that an irregularity meant only a procedural defect.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that irregularity is not limited to procedural defects and includes a failure to act in the manner prescribed by the statute, including use of the wrong valuation method.
issues.legal_principle: The ordinary meaning of “irregularity” in section 131(2)(b) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923 is not restricted to procedural defects; it covers a failure to do something in the manner laid down by the statute. The Court adopted the approach in Corporation of Calcutta v. Chandoo Lal Bhai Chand Modi, 57 C.W.N. 882, and agreed with the relevant observation in North British & Mercantile Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, Case No. 6 of 1943 (unreported).

predicates.municipal_valuation_challenge: A ratepayer challenged a municipal authority’s valuation of property.
predicates.prescribed_valuation_method_not_followed: The municipal authority used a method other than the method applicable to the property.

issues.definition: When a ratepayer challenges a municipal valuation and the prescribed valuation method was not followed, use of the wrong method is an irregularity.
